lessons.title: Welcome to BE102!
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
BE102 teaches you to build a real web server and API in Python with Flask: the backend that games and tools talk to. The practice project is My Movies.

KEY IDEAS
1. Unit 1: a first web server.
2. Unit 2: API structure (URLs and JSON).
3. Unit 3: CRUD (create, read, update, delete).
4. Unit 4: documentation and polish so others can use the API.
5. The same skills power shops, player data, feeds and tasks, and later let you put AI behind your own API and control when it's called.

KEY POINTS
- Flask = a Python framework for building web servers and APIs.

lessons.title: Backend roles and what a server does
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The frontend (client) shows the interface, handles input and sends requests. The backend (server) receives requests, processes them and returns responses.

KEY IDEAS
1. Frontend: what the user sees (UI, buttons, text); handles clicks and input; sends requests and updates the screen with the answers.
2. Backend: receives a request, applies rules, checks, calculations and data lookups, and returns a response (data, success or error).

KEY POINTS
- The frontend handles the user interface; the backend receives requests, processes them and returns responses.

lessons.title: The request-response cycle
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Every call is: the client asks, the server decides, the server answers. The client writes the request (method, URL, body); the server writes the response (status code, body).

KEY IDEAS
1. Client = consumer (a game or any app using the API). Server = producer (the backend).
2. Request: method (get data or change something), URL (where it goes), body (data sent, like an item to buy).
3. Response: status code (did it work?), body (data sent back).
4. Both sides also send headers, like Content-Type, which says what kind of data the body holds.

KEY POINTS
- Client → method, URL, request body. Server → status code, response body.

lessons.title: Isolating projects with venv
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A virtual environment gives each project its own Python and packages, so one project's upgrades can't break another.

STEPS (POWERSHELL)
1. Create: py -m venv venv
2. Activate: .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 → (venv) appears in the prompt.
3. Check: Get-Command python → the path points inside the project's venv.
4. Deactivate: deactivate

KEY POINTS
- Each project has its own Python tools, chosen when you activate it.
- Experiments and upgrades stay inside one project.

lessons.title: Installing Flask with pip
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Install → freeze → restore. pip install flask installs into the active venv only. pip freeze > requirements.txt saves the exact versions. pip install -r requirements.txt rebuilds the same setup somewhere else.

STEPS
1. Check (venv) is in the prompt.
2. pip install flask
3. pip freeze shows every package with its exact version (Flask==3.1.3, Werkzeug==3.1.8, ...).
4. pip freeze > requirements.txt saves that list in the project folder.
5. Elsewhere, in a new active venv: pip install -r requirements.txt

KEY POINTS
- Installing without (venv) puts packages in the system Python instead.
- > sends the output into a file.

lessons.title: Your first Flask app
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The smallest Flask app: import Flask, create app = Flask(__name__), and call app.run(debug=True). It listens on http://127.0.0.1:5000. A 404 at / is fine, because there are no routes yet. Ctrl + C stops it. Debug mode restarts the server when you save.

KEY IDEAS
1. Your code: import Flask, create the app object, start the server.
2. Flask: listens on the port, reads HTTP requests, matches URLs to routes, sends responses.
3. A running server loaded your code once. Without debug mode, changes need a stop and restart.
4. Debug mode watches your files and reloads on save ("Detected change in ... reloading").

CODE
```python
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

if __name__ == "__main__":       # only when this file is run directly
    app.run(debug=True)
```

```powershell
cd movies
python app.py                    # or: python -m flask run --debug
# Ctrl + C to stop
```

KEY POINTS
- 404 at / means the server is running but has no routes yet.
- No debug: edit → save → stop → rerun. Debug: edit → save → automatic reload.

lessons.title: Defining routes and URL paths
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
@app.route("/path") connects a URL to the view function right below it. Whatever the function returns is what the browser shows. print() only shows in your terminal.

KEY IDEAS
1. Route decorator: "when someone requests /path, run the function below me."
2. View function: the function that handles that URL.
3. return → the response body the browser displays. print → the terminal only, for debugging.

CODE
```python
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/")
def home():
    return "Hello Movies API"

@app.route("/about")
def about():
    print("Inside about route")          # terminal only
    return "About this Movies API"       # shown in the browser

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)
```

KEY POINTS
- /  → "Hello Movies API". /about → "About this Movies API".
- flask run finds a file named app.py on its own. To point it elsewhere in PowerShell: $env:FLASK_APP = "file.py" (set FLASK_APP=... is Command Prompt syntax).

lessons.title: Returning text and HTML
Returning JSON with jsonify
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
jsonify(data) turns a Python dict or list into real JSON and sets Content-Type: application/json. Static routes return the same data every time; dynamic routes build it with logic, like random.choice(movies).

CODE
```python
import random
from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/movie")
def movie():
    movies = [
        {"title": "Jaws", "year": 1975, "rating": 4.5},
        {"title": "Alien", "year": 1979, "rating": 5.0},
    ]
    return jsonify(random.choice(movies))
```

```text
jsonify(data) → {"title":"Jaws"}     Content-Type: application/json  (valid JSON)
str(data)     → {'title': 'Jaws'}    Content-Type: text/html         (not JSON: single quotes)
```

KEY POINTS
- APIs always return real JSON.
- Static = the same data every time. Dynamic = built by logic per request.
- Since Flask 1.1, returning a dict directly also gives JSON.

CORRECTION
The lesson said str(data) is sent as text/plain. Checked by running it: Flask sends any returned string as text/html. The body still isn't JSON, which is the real problem.

lessons.title: Exploring a real API service with Swagger
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A local script only runs on your machine. An HTTP API service has URLs that any client can call: "Python is internal, HTTP is a service." Swagger's interactive docs for the Petstore API can send real requests and show the data's schema.

KEY IDEAS
1. URL: the address of a resource, like https://petstore.swagger.io/v2/pet/1.
2. Swagger shows each operation's method, path, parameters, request body and response.
3. POST sends a JSON body to create something. GET reads data, usually with URL parameters and no body.
4. Schema (model): the blueprint of the data: fields, types, and which are required (marked *).
5. 2xx = success. 4xx = the client made a mistake.

CODE
```text
POST https://petstore.swagger.io/v2/pet           body: {"name": "dolphin", "photoUrls": ["string"], "status": "available", ...}
GET  https://petstore.swagger.io/v2/pet/findByStatus?status=available   → 200, an array of pets

Pet {
  id
  category  Category { ... }
  name*
  photoUrls*
  tags
  status
}
```

KEY POINTS
- An internal script has no URL; an API service is reachable over HTTP.
- JSON APIs and HTML pages both use URLs, but an API returns data, not a page.

lessons.title: Choosing what your API returns
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A response format is the body plus its Content-Type header. HTML (text/html) is for people in browsers; JSON (application/json) is for games, AI and scripts. A JSON body labelled text/html breaks the API's contract, and the client may not parse it.

KEY IDEAS
1. Browser user → HTML body, Content-Type: text/html.
2. Game, AI or script → JSON body, Content-Type: application/json.
3. Very simple human messages → Content-Type: text/plain.
4. API contract: the Content-Type promises what the body really is.

CODE
```text
Wrong: body {"health": 80, "mana": 30}   Content-Type: text/html
Right: body {"health": 80, "mana": 30}   Content-Type: application/json
```

KEY POINTS
- HTML is for humans, JSON is for programs.
- If the body is JSON, the Content-Type must say application/json.

lessons.title: REST principles and resources
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
REST thinks in nouns (resources: movie, player, quest), not verbs (create, join, buy). A resource has a shape: fields, types, and which ones are required, which is a product decision. Resource URLs are nouns (/movies); action URLs start with verbs (/createQuest).

KEY IDEAS
1. Resource: a thing you can put "a" or "the" before (a movie, a player).
2. Action: something you can put "to" before (to create, to ban).
3. Resource shape: e.g. title (string, required), year (number, required), genre (string, optional), rating (number, optional).
4. Resource-oriented URLs: /movies, /players, /players/search (search treated as a sub-resource).
5. Action-oriented URLs: /createQuest, /rateMovie, /banPlayer.

STEPS: DESIGN FROM A STORY
1. Highlight the nouns → candidate resources.
2. Highlight the verbs → candidate actions.
3. Give each resource 3–5 fields and decide required or optional by what the app must always know.

KEY POINTS
- A URL starting with a verb is action-style; nouns (or noun/noun) are resource-style.
- "Endpoint" isn't a domain noun; it's just the path.

lessons.title: Resource URLs and HTTP methods
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A collection URL is /movies and an item URL is /movies/{id}. The path stays a noun, and the HTTP method is the action: GET reads, POST creates (the server picks the id), PUT replaces a known item, DELETE removes it.

CODE
```text
Read all            → GET    /movies
Read one            → GET    /movies/{id}
Create new          → POST   /movies
Replace one         → PUT    /movies/{id}
Delete one          → DELETE /movies/{id}

/getAllMovies          → GET    /movies
/createPlayer          → POST   /players
/deleteMovie/7         → DELETE /movies/7
/updatePlayerScore/15  → PUT    /players/15
/getMovieById/10       → GET    /movies/10
```

KEY POINTS
- URL = nouns; method = action.
- Add something new to the list → POST /collection. Replace a known id → PUT /collection/{id}.
- Words like get, create, update, delete or fetch in a path are a sign the action belongs in the method.
- PATCH changes only some fields; this course uses PUT for updates.

lessons.title: Statelessness and server memory
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A stateless server doesn't remember callers between requests. Every request is a stranger, so it must carry everything it needs: the resource, the id and the filters. Shared data in memory is fine; remembering each caller isn't. Benefit: any server can handle any request.

KEY IDEAS
1. Self-contained request: /movies (resource), /movies/10 (id), ?rating=pg13 (filters).
2. Allowed: shared data the process holds while running (the movies list).
3. Not allowed as state: per-caller history ("this player last asked for PG-13").
4. Stateless servers scale out easily (add servers) and recover easily (another server takes over).

KEY POINTS
- The server doesn't remember callers; each request carries what it needs.
- Any server can handle the next request.

lessons.title: Creating an in-memory data store
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Start a new project with its own environment, then define the movies list as seed data. The list lives in memory, so anything added while running is gone after a restart; only what's written in app.py comes back.

STEPS (POWERSHELL)
1. mkdir movies_api, then cd movies_api
2. python -m venv venv
3. venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
4. pip install flask
5. pip freeze > requirements.txt

CODE
```python
movies = [
    {"id": 1, "title": "The Matrix", "director": "The Wachowskis", "year": 1999, "watched": True},
    {"id": 2, "title": "Spirited Away", "director": "Hayao Miyazaki", "year": 2001, "watched": False},
    {"id": 3, "title": "Inception", "director": "Christopher Nolan", "year": 2010, "watched": True},
]
```

KEY POINTS
- Fields: id (unique integer), title, director, year, watched (True/False).
- In-memory data resets on restart: it's rebuilt from the code, and anything added only in memory is lost.
- Permanent change → edit app.py. Temporary change → only while it runs.

lessons.title: Reading the collection
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
GET /movies returns the whole list as JSON. The home route serves index.html, and that page calls /movies to show the cards. print() goes to the console; return goes to the client.

CODE
```python
from flask import Flask, jsonify, send_file

app = Flask(__name__)
movies = [...]                      # the in-memory list

@app.get("/")
def home():
    return send_file("index.html")  # index.html sits next to app.py

@app.get("/movies")
def get_movies():
    return jsonify(movies)          # list of dicts → JSON array

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)
```

STEPS: VERIFY
1. python app.py → "Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000".
2. /movies → a JSON array with status 200.
3. / → the My Movies page shows the cards.

KEY POINTS
- Collection endpoint: GET /movies returns every movie.
- The client only ever sees what you return.

lessons.title: Filtering with query parameters
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Query parameters (?key=value) let one endpoint filter optionally. request.args.get("director") returns None when the parameter is missing, so nothing crashes. No parameter → the full list. No match → an empty list.

CODE
```python
from flask import request

@app.get("/movies")
def get_movies():
    director = request.args.get("director")
    if director:
        return jsonify([m for m in movies if m["director"] == director])
    return jsonify(movies)
```

```text
/movies                                → all movies
/movies?director=Christopher+Nolan     → only Inception
/movies?director=DoesNotExist          → []   (still 200, no crash)
```

KEY POINTS
- Query parameters live in request.args.
- .get() returns None for a missing parameter instead of raising an error.
- In a URL, + or %20 stands for a space.

lessons.title: Reading an item by ID
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A path parameter picks one item: @app.get("/movies/<int:movie_id>") passes the number in. Find it and return it, or return a JSON 404. The path says which item; the query says how to filter a list. Use /movies/3, not /movies?id=3.

CODE
```python
@app.get("/movies/<int:movie_id>")
def get_movie(movie_id):
    movie = next((m for m in movies if m["id"] == movie_id), None)
    if movie is None:
        return jsonify({"error": "Movie not found"}), 404
    return jsonify(movie), 200
```

```text
/movies/3                 → one movie (path = which item)
/movies?watched=true      → filtered list (query = how)
/movies/9999              → 404 {"error": "Movie not found"}
```

KEY POINTS
- <int:movie_id> only matches whole numbers and hands them over as int.
- Keep the error shape consistent ("error" key) across the API.
- Watch the spelling: /movies/2, not /movie/2.

lessons.title: Testing read endpoints in Postman
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Postman: pick the method, type the URL, click Send, then check both the status and the JSON body. Save working requests in a collection so you can retest after every restart.

STEPS
1. Method: GET. URL: http://localhost:5000/...
2. Send.
3. Check the status (200 or 404) and the body's shape (array, object or error).
4. Save it to the collection; duplicate and edit it for the next test.

CODE
```text
GET /movies                              → 200, JSON array
GET /movies/1                            → 200, one JSON object
GET /movies?director=Christopher+Nolan   → 200, filtered array (Inception)
GET /movies/999                          → 404, {"error": "Movie not found"}
```

KEY POINTS
- Always check the status and the body.
- Postman shows what the route returns, never what it prints.
- Saved requests in "My Movies API – Read" are one-click retests.

lessons.title: Write requests: GET versus POST
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
GET is read-only (safe), and its data goes in the URL. POST is for writing, and its data goes in the request body. Flask matches path + method: a route with methods=["POST"] answers a GET with 405 Method Not Allowed. A path that doesn't exist gives 404.

KEY IDEAS
1. Read (safe): only returns data, changes nothing.
2. Write: sends data the server stores or uses to change something.
3. GET data lives in the URL: /movies?director=Nolan.
4. POST data lives in the body: {"title": "New Movie", "director": "Nolan"}.

CODE
```python
@app.route("/echo", methods=["POST"])
def echo_post():
    return {"message": "Received POST on /echo"}
```

```text
POST /echo  → 200
GET  /echo  → 405 Method Not Allowed (path exists, method not allowed)
GET  /nope  → 404 Not Found (path doesn't exist)
```

KEY POINTS
- 404 = no such path. 405 = the path exists but not for that method.
- %0A in a URL is a hidden newline. /echo%0A doesn't match /echo, so it gave 404 instead of 405.

lessons.title: Reading a JSON request body
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The client sends JSON in a POST body with Content-Type: application/json, and Flask reads it with request.get_json(), which gives you a Python dict. Bad JSON → 400. Missing or wrong Content-Type → 415.

KEY IDEAS
1. Whole objects (a movie, a save, a score) travel as JSON in the body, not in the query string.
2. Content-Type: application/json tells the server how to read the body.
3. request.get_json(silent=True) returns None instead of raising Flask's error, so your own validation can answer.

CODE
```python
from flask import request, jsonify

@app.post("/movies/body-test")
def movie_body_test():
    content_type = request.headers.get("Content-Type")
    data = request.get_json(silent=True)
    title = data.get("title") if isinstance(data, dict) else None
    return jsonify({"seen_content_type": content_type, "raw_data": data, "got_title": title})
```

```text
POST /movies HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Inception", "year": 2010}
```

KEY POINTS
- To send JSON that get_json() reads, use POST with a JSON body.
- With plain get_json() in Flask 3: invalid JSON → 400, wrong Content-Type → 415.

lessons.title: Building a POST endpoint
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A POST endpoint reads the request body (JSON from the client) with request.get_json() and sends back a response body built with jsonify. Every request, whatever its method, gets a response.

CODE
```python
@app.post("/movies")
def create_movie():
    data = request.get_json(silent=True)
    return jsonify({"message": "Got your movie", "received": data})
```

```json
{"title": "Godot RPG", "director": "You", "year": 2026, "watched": false}
```

KEY POINTS
- Request body: JSON the client sends to the server.
- Response body: JSON the server sends back.
- Request/response is about direction; GET/POST is about intent.

lessons.title: CRUD pt 1: Creating resources with POST
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Create: read the JSON, pick the next id, build the new movie, append it to the list, and return it with 201 Created. The page sees 201, clears the form and reloads the list with GET /movies.

STEPS
1. data = request.get_json(silent=True)
2. Pick a server-side id.
3. Build the movie dict from the body.
4. movies.append(new_movie)
5. return jsonify(new_movie), 201
6. Front end: on 201, reset the form and call GET /movies again.

CODE
```python
@app.post("/movies")
def create_movie():
    data = request.get_json(silent=True)
    next_id = max((m["id"] for m in movies), default=0) + 1
    new_movie = {
        "id": next_id,
        "title": data["title"],
        "director": data["director"],
        "year": data["year"],
        "watched": data["watched"],
    }
    movies.append(new_movie)
    return jsonify(new_movie), 201
```

```javascript
const { status } = await api("POST", "/movies", body);
if (status === 201) {
  f.reset();      // clear the form
  load();         // GET /movies and redraw the cards
}
```

KEY POINTS
- The server picks the id, never the client.
- A body without "title" raises KeyError → 500. Lesson 5 adds validation.
- GET has no body and changes nothing; POST has a body and creates something.

CORRECTION
Checked by running it:
- The GET code had a stray } line, which is a Python SyntaxError. It's removed.
- max() of an empty list crashes (ValueError → 500) once every movie is deleted. default=0 fixes it.
- Taking the highest id + 1 reuses the id of a deleted newest movie. A counter that only goes up, like next_item_id in Lesson 10, never reuses ids.

lessons.title: Validating input and the 400 response
CRUD pt 2: Updating with PUT
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
PUT /movies/<id> replaces an existing movie: validate the same way as POST, find it (404 if missing), build the full new dict with the same id, put it in place, and return 200. Sending the same PUT twice gives the same result: PUT is idempotent.

STEPS
1. Validate the body exactly like POST → 400 on any problem.
2. Find the movie's index → 404 if not found.
3. Build the full replacement with the same id.
4. movies[index] = updated_movie
5. return jsonify(updated_movie), 200

CODE
```python
@app.put("/movies/<int:movie_id>")
def update_movie(movie_id):
    # ...same validation as POST → year_value...
    index = next((i for i, m in enumerate(movies) if m["id"] == movie_id), None)
    if index is None:
        return jsonify({"error": "Not Found", "message": "Movie not found"}), 404
    updated = {"id": movie_id, "title": data["title"], "director": data["director"],
               "year": year_value, "watched": data["watched"]}
    movies[index] = updated
    return jsonify(updated), 200
```

KEY POINTS
- POST /movies creates and assigns an id. PUT /movies/<id> replaces, keeping the id.
- Idempotent: repeating the request leaves the same end state.

lessons.title: CRUD pt 3: Deleting with DELETE
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
DELETE /movies/<id>: find the index, remove it with movies.pop(index), and return "", 204 (success, no body). Missing → 404 with JSON. Deleting twice leaves the same end state, so DELETE is idempotent even though the second call returns 404.

CODE
```python
@app.delete("/movies/<int:movie_id>")
def delete_movie(movie_id):
    index = next((i for i, m in enumerate(movies) if m["id"] == movie_id), None)
    if index is None:
        return jsonify({"error": "Movie not found"}), 404
    movies.pop(index)
    return "", 204
```

KEY POINTS
- 200: success with a JSON body. 201: created. 204: success, no body. 404: doesn't exist.
- enumerate gives both the index and the item, and the index is what pop needs.
- Idempotent: after one or two DELETEs, the movie is gone either way.

lessons.title: Mapping the full CRUD surface
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
The full CRUD map: create with POST /movies → 201; read with GET /movies or /movies/<id> → 200; update with PUT /movies/<id> → 200; delete with DELETE /movies/<id> → 204. 404 is an error, never a success.

CODE
```text
CRUD action      | Method | URL           | Success        | Meaning
-----------------|--------|---------------|----------------|----------------------------
Create movie     | POST   | /movies       | 201 Created    | new movie made
Read all movies  | GET    | /movies       | 200 OK         | list in the body
Read one movie   | GET    | /movies/<id>  | 200 OK         | one movie in the body
Update movie     | PUT    | /movies/<id>  | 200 OK         | updated movie in the body
Delete movie     | DELETE | /movies/<id>  | 204 No Content | deleted, no body
```

KEY POINTS
- Collection URL (/movies): POST and GET. Item URL (/movies/<id>): GET, PUT, DELETE.
- POST is create, not update. Reads use 200, not 201. A successful delete is 204, not 404.
- The same map works for /players, /items, /monsters.

lessons.title: Verifying the CRUD lifecycle in Postman
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Drive one movie through its whole life in Postman: POST (201 + new id) → GET (200) → PUT (200) → GET shows the change → DELETE (204) → GET (404). After a server restart, the in-memory list is back to the seed movies.

STEPS
1. POST /movies with a full JSON body → 201 and the new id.
2. GET /movies/<id> → 200, that movie.
3. PUT /movies/<id> with every field changed → 200, the updated movie.
4. GET /movies/<id> → 200, shows the changes.
5. DELETE /movies/<id> → 204, empty body.
6. GET /movies/<id> → 404, {"error": "Movie not found"}.
7. Restart the server → GET /movies shows only the seed movies.

KEY POINTS
- POST → 201. GET and PUT → 200. DELETE → 204. Missing id → 404. Bad body → 400.
- Changes live in memory until the server restarts.
- Track the id carefully between steps.

lessons.title: Challenge: build a CRUD resource
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Build your own CRUD resource: items (name, type, rarity and power required; description optional) at /items and /items/<int:item_id>. The in-memory list uses a next_item_id counter, the same validation pattern, and the same status codes: 201, 200, 204, 400 and 404.

KEY IDEAS
1. Required: name, type, rarity (non-empty strings), power (number). Optional: description.
2. Collection: /items. Item: /items/<int:item_id>. No verbs in the path.
3. A counter that only goes up never reuses an id.

CODE
```python
items = []
next_item_id = 1

@app.post("/items")
def create_item():
    global next_item_id                  # needed to change the module-level counter
    data = request.get_json(silent=True)
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        return bad_request("Request body must be a JSON object.")
    for field in ("name", "type", "rarity", "power"):
        if field not in data:
            return bad_request(f"Missing required field: {field}")
    # ...string checks for name, type, rarity...
    try:
        power_value = int(data["power"])
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return bad_request("Field 'power' must be a number.")
    new_item = {
        "id": next_item_id,
        "name": data["name"],
        "type": data["type"],
        "rarity": data["rarity"],
        "power": power_value,
        "description": data.get("description", ""),
    }
    items.append(new_item)
    next_item_id += 1
    return jsonify(new_item), 201
```

```json
{"name": "plunger", "type": "sword", "rarity": "very common", "power": 1,
 "description": "Gross go put that back by the TOILET!"}
```

KEY POINTS
- POST /items → 201 or 400. GET /items → 200 ([] when empty). GET /items/<id> → 200 or 404.
- PUT /items/<id> → 200, 400 or 404. DELETE /items/<id> → 204 or 404.

NOTE
Changing next_item_id inside a function needs global next_item_id, or Python raises UnboundLocalError ("cannot access local variable").

lessons.title: Generating Swagger documentation
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Flasgger adds a /docs/ page that lists your endpoints and lets you test them with "Try it out". Document a route with a docstring: a summary line, ---, then YAML for parameters and responses. The docs only describe your API; they don't change what it does.

STEPS
1. pip install flasgger
2. Set app.config["SWAGGER"], then swagger = Swagger(app), after creating the app and before the routes.
3. Run the app and open http://localhost:5000/docs/ (with the trailing slash).
4. "No operations defined in spec!" means Swagger works but nothing is documented yet.
5. Add a docstring to a route, restart, and use Try it out → Execute.

CODE
```python
from flask import Flask, jsonify
from flasgger import Swagger

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config["SWAGGER"] = {"title": "Movies API", "uiversion": 3, "specs_route": "/docs/"}
swagger = Swagger(app)

@app.get("/items/<int:item_id>")
def get_item(item_id):
    '''
    Get one item by ID
    ---
    parameters:
      - name: item_id
        in: path
        type: integer
        required: true
        description: ID of the item
    responses:
      200:
        description: The item data
      404:
        description: Item not found
    '''
    ...
```

KEY POINTS
- Endpoint = HTTP method + path.
- Swagger is the map and test panel; the route code is the actual behavior.
- Everything after --- in the docstring is Swagger YAML.

lessons.title: Challenge: harden a new endpoint
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A hardened PUT /movies/<int:movie_id>/watched: the body must be an object, "watched" must be present and true/false, then find the movie (200) or return 404. Every error uses the same {"error", "message"} shape, and every path is tested.

STEPS
1. Body not a JSON object → 400.
2. "watched" missing → 400.
3. "watched" not a boolean → 400.
4. Movie not found → 404.
5. Update and return the movie → 200.

CODE
```python
@app.put("/movies/<int:movie_id>/watched")
def update_movie_watched(movie_id):
    data = request.get_json(silent=True)
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        return jsonify({"error": "Bad Request", "message": "Request body must be a JSON object."}), 400
    if "watched" not in data:
        return jsonify({"error": "Bad Request", "message": "Missing required field: watched"}), 400
    if not isinstance(data["watched"], bool):
        return jsonify({"error": "Bad Request",
                        "message": "Field 'watched' must be a boolean (true or false)."}), 400
    for movie in movies:
        if movie["id"] == movie_id:
            movie["watched"] = data["watched"]
            return jsonify(movie), 200
    return jsonify({"error": "Not Found", "message": f"Movie with id {movie_id} not found."}), 404
```

```text
PUT /movies/2/watched   {"watched": true}    → 200, updated movie
PUT /movies/2/watched   {"watched": "yes"}   → 400, must be a boolean
PUT /movies/2/watched   {}                   → 400, missing watched
PUT /movies/999/watched {"watched": true}    → 404
```

KEY POINTS
- The same guard-clause pattern works for any update endpoint.
- Test the failure paths, not just the happy one.

lessons.title: Challenge: document a new endpoint
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Document the hardened endpoint so /docs matches reality: the path parameter (in: path), the body parameter (in: body with a schema), and every status you return (200, 400, 404). Then loop: edit → restart → Try it out → compare the live responses with the docs.

STEPS
1. Write the docstring: parameters and responses.
2. Restart Flask.
3. Open /docs and find PUT /movies/{movie_id}/watched.
4. Try it out: a valid body (200), a bad body (400), a bad id (404).
5. Each live status and JSON should match the docs. If not, fix the docs.

CODE
```python
@app.put("/movies/<int:movie_id>/watched")
def update_movie_watched(movie_id):
    '''
    Update watched status for a movie
    ---
    parameters:
      - name: movie_id
        in: path
        type: integer
        required: true
      - name: body
        in: body
        required: true
        schema:
          type: object
          required: [watched]
          properties:
            watched:
              type: boolean
    responses:
      200:
        description: Movie updated
        schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            id: {type: integer}
            title: {type: string}
            director: {type: string}
            year: {type: integer}
            watched: {type: boolean}
      400:
        description: Invalid body
        schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            error: {type: string}
            message: {type: string}
      404:
        description: Movie not found
        schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            error: {type: string}
            message: {type: string}
    '''
    ...
```

KEY POINTS
- Path parameter: part of the URL. Body parameter: the JSON sent.
- Mistakes to avoid: two --- lines, requestBody instead of in: body, a code path with no return, code after a return.

CORRECTION
The lesson's docstring mixed two versions of the spec. Flasgger uses Swagger 2.0 by default (why in: body works and requestBody doesn't). In 2.0 a path parameter uses type: integer directly, and a response uses schema: right under the status code, not content: application/json: schema: (that's OpenAPI 3). The docstring above is all 2.0, so the response shapes show in the docs.

lessons.title: The REST API contract end to end
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
A REST API is a contract: the same method + URL + body always gives a predictable status + JSON. Trace any request from intention → method → URL → handler → status + JSON.

CODE
```text
Read list   → GET    /api/movies       → 200, [ movie, ... ]
Read one    → GET    /api/movies/:id   → 200 movie | 404 {"error": "Movie not found"}
Create      → POST   /api/movies       → 201, new movie with id
Update      → PUT    /api/movies/:id   → 200 updated movie | 404
Delete      → DELETE /api/movies/:id   → 204 no body | 404
```

KEY POINTS
- Noun URLs (/api/movies, /api/movies/:id), never verbs (/api/delete-movie/4).
- Methods match intent; status codes carry meaning.
- Errors are JSON with the right status, never a 200 with "does not exist".
- Create has no id in the URL; the server makes one.

lessons.title: Capstone: build and document an API
Challenge: diagnose a broken API
lessons.refined:
IN PLAIN WORDS
Diagnose an API that breaks the rules: verb URLs, wrong status codes, missing validation, mixed error shapes. Fix it with nouns in URLs, one error shape everywhere, and the right 4xx for each problem.

STEPS: PICK THE 4XX
1. Wrong URL or missing resource → 404.
2. Real URL, method not allowed → 405.
3. Malformed body or missing fields → 400.
4. Clashes with existing data (duplicate username) → 409.
5. Valid JSON that breaks a rule (level 0 when the minimum is 1) → 422.

CODE
```text
Create message → POST   /messages
List messages  → GET    /messages
One message    → GET    /messages/{id}
Delete message → DELETE /messages/{id}
```

```json
{"error": "validation_failed", "message": "text must be at least 1 character"}
```

KEY POINTS
- Nouns in URLs, verbs in methods.
- One error format, used everywhere.
- 400 vs 422 is a convention, not a law. Many APIs (including your movies and spells APIs) use 400 for every validation error. Be consistent.
